organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Controls all 34 provinces and has over 100,000 fighters, plus US-supplied materiel. Pakistan is its state sponsor and Iran does so to a lesser degree. Shelters al-Qaeda, AQIS, TTP and Jamaat Ansarullah.

organizations.name: Islamic State Khorasan Province
organizations.notes: Formed in about 2015 from ex-TTP members, disaffected Afghan Taliban and a few al-Qaeda members. Controls no territory and operates in cells. UN estimates it has several thousand fighters. Strongholds were previously Nangarhar and Kunar. Ran an April 2022 campaign called 'Revenge of the Two Sheikhs'.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Operates in Afghanistan under Taliban protection and is led by Zawahiri. Its branches flourish particularly in Africa.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent
organizations.notes: al-Qaeda's South Asia branch, sheltered by the Taliban.

organizations.name: Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan
aliases: Movement of the Taliban in Pakistan
organizations.notes: Thousands of fighters are in Afghanistan with safe haven and conduct cross-border attacks. Attacks reportedly doubled in a year. Aims to create an Islamic Emirate of Pakistan. Controlled large parts of northwestern Pakistan from 2006 to about 2015-16.

organizations.name: Jamaat Ansarullah
organizations.notes: Tajik terror group. The Taliban put its Tajik leader in charge of five districts in northern Afghanistan in summer 2021.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Operates on both sides of the border; its headquarters were in Miranshah, North Waziristan, for two decades.

organizations.name: Pakistani military and intelligence establishment
organizations.notes: Together with the military, it is the 'deep state' that controls foreign policy and backs the Afghan Taliban for strategic depth.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula
organizations.notes: Controlled territory in southern Yemen in 2011-12 and again in 2015-16. Currently on a downward path but not defeated.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: Controlled most of southern and central Somalia, including Mogadishu, c. 2007-2012. Was driven out by an African Union mission with US help. Now said to control at least 25% of Somalia and is rising.

organizations.name: US Navy SEALs and CIA
organizations.notes: Carried out the Abbottabad raid that killed bin Laden.

organizations.name: Afghan National Army
organizations.notes: Former Afghan government forces, now defunct. Their US-provided weapons fell to the Taliban.

places.name: Kunduz

places.name: Nangarhar
places.significance: Former ISKP stronghold in eastern Afghanistan.

places.name: Kunar
places.significance: Former ISKP stronghold; also hit by Pakistani airstrikes.

places.name: Khost
places.significance: Hit by Pakistani airstrikes in April/May 2022.

places.name: Uzbekistan
places.significance: Target of the first ISKP mortar/rocket attack launched from Afghanistan against another country, April 2022.

places.name: Abbottabad
places.significance: City near Pakistan's military academy where bin Laden lived in a large compound until the 2011 raid.

places.name: Miranshah

places.name: North Waziristan

places.name: Durand Line
places.significance: Border not recognized by the Pashtuns who straddle it.

key_claims: The Taliban control all 34 Afghan provinces and shelter al-Qaeda, AQIS, TTP and Jamaat Ansarullah, contradicting their claim to bar foreign terrorists.
ISKP controls no territory and operates in cells, so it is mostly a nuisance to the Taliban, but its attacks challenge Taliban claims of full control.
ISKP's April 2022 attacks hit Hazara, Shia and Sufi targets and included its first cross-border mortar attack, on Uzbekistan.
Pakistan backs the Afghan Taliban for 'strategic depth' against India and tolerates TTP violence as the price, so open Pakistan-Taliban conflict over the airstrikes is unlikely.
The Hakkanis and Hafiz Gul Bahadur are examples of how Pashtun militants straddle the Durand Line, part of what Tom Joscelyn called the 'wheel of jihad'.
Bin Laden's killing did not collapse al-Qaeda; Zawahiri led it through the rise of ISIS and its branches in Africa are flourishing.
Bin Laden lived in Abbottabad for years, which shows Pakistani duplicity; the US did not tell Pakistan about the raid.
Khalilzad's calling Pakistan a 'partner in peace' was either a lie or a cynical ploy.
